definitions.text: The pleasant, earthy scent that follows rain falling on dry soil.
definitions.example: First rain in a month and the whole street smelled of petrichor; even the Barkeep paused mid-grumble.

origin: Coined in 1964 by researchers Isabel Bear and Richard Thomas from Greek petra (stone) and ichor, the golden fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods.

definitions.text: The realization that every passerby is living a life as vivid and complicated as your own.
definitions.example: Moment of sonder on the packed night bus: every tired face on it has a favorite mug, probably.

origin: Popularized by John Koenig's The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows (2012), built on German sonder- (special, as in Sondersache, 'special case') and echoing French sonder, 'to probe.'

definitions.text: Excessively or foolishly fond of one's wife.
definitions.example: Martin is so uxorious he apologizes to his wife's houseplants when he forgets to water them.

origin: From Latin uxorius, 'of a wife,' from uxor (wife). In Latin it flattered; in English it soon picked up a teasing edge of 'too much.'

definitions.text: Jumbled together in total disorder.
definitions.example: The regulars' coats on the tavern hooks hang higgledy-piggledy, three scarves deep.

definitions.text: In a confused, messy, any-which-way manner.

origin: Recorded since the 1500s, one of English's many reduplications in the family of willy-nilly and hocus-pocus. The pig in the middle is nonsense, which has never once stopped English.

definitions.text: To throw someone or something out of a window.
definitions.example: The Barkeep has threatened to defenestrate the jukebox after every fourth bagpipe track.

origin: From Latin de- (down from) + fenestra (window), coined around 1618 for the Defenestration of Prague, when two imperial officials were thrown from a castle window and, astonishingly, lived.

definitions.text: The happy accident of finding something good when you weren't looking for it.
definitions.example: Found a tenner in my coat on the way to the tavern. Serendipity, and it bought the first round.

definitions.text: Lucky chance; good fortune that arrives unplanned.

origin: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754 from the fairy tale The Three Princes of Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka, whose heroes kept stumbling into fortunate discoveries.

definitions.text: To deliberately make something unclear or confusing.
To darken, cloud, or obscure, literally or figuratively.

origin: From Latin obfuscatus, 'darkened,' from ob- (over) + fuscus (dark). To obfuscate is to throw a shadow over the facts and hope nobody brings a lamp.

definitions.text: Sweet and smooth to the ear; flowing like honey.
definitions.example: The singer's mellifluous low notes hushed even the dart corner.

origin: From Latin mellifluus, 'flowing with honey,' from mel (honey) + fluere (to flow). Marmalade passes through the same honeyed Latin root on its way from quince to toast.

definitions.text: Habitually complaining, in a whiny or petulant tone.
Fretful and peevish; never quite satisfied.

origin: From Latin querulus, 'full of complaints,' from queri (to complain, lament). The whine is baked into the syllables.

definitions.text: Calm composure in a crisis; cool self-possession.
definitions.example: When the keg hissed like a snake, the Barkeep handled it with pure sangfroid and one raised eyebrow.

origin: Borrowed from French, literally 'cold blood.' English has cold feet and cold shoulders; the French kept the useful kind of cold.

definitions.text: To leave suddenly and secretly, typically to avoid capture or responsibility.
definitions.example: Someone absconded with the last slice of pie, and frankly we respect the commitment.

origin: From Latin abscondere, 'to hide away,' from abs- (away) + condere (to hide, store). A word for leaving with your hat low and your reasons lower.

definitions.text: Relating to the countryside; idyllically rural and peaceful.
Of or concerning shepherds and pastoral life.

origin: From Latin bucolicus, from Greek boukolikos, 'of a cowherd,' from bous (cow). Pastoral poetry wearing a toga and muddy boots.

definitions.text: Keenly perceptive; quick to grasp the truth of things.
definitions.example: Perspicacious of you to notice the Barkeep waters the good whiskey on Tuesdays.

origin: From Latin perspicax, 'sharp-sighted,' from perspicere (to see through). Conspicuous is a cousin: both about seeing, one clearly and one glaringly.

definitions.text: Lacking energy, enthusiasm, or effort.
Casually careless; going through the motions.

origin: From the old sigh 'lackaday!' — short for alack the day — as if the word itself were too weary to finish the sentence.

definitions.text: Lasting a very short time; fleeting.
definitions.example: The head on a bad pour is ephemeral; on a good one it lingers like gossip.

origin: From Greek ephemeros, 'lasting but a day,' from epi- (on) + hemera (day). The mayfly is the word's patron saint.

definitions.text: Stubbornly resistant to authority or control.
Hard to manage or work with; mulish.

origin: From Latin recalcitrare, 'to kick back,' from re- (back) + calcitrare (to kick), from calx (heel). A mule in word form.

definitions.text: Excessively particular about details, cleanliness, or correctness.
definitions.example: He is fastidious about his pint: the glass room-temperature, never chilled, and do not ask why.

origin: From Latin fastidiosus, 'squeamish, disdainful,' from fastidium (disgust). It once meant 'loathsome'; the meaning flipped to describe the easily disgusted.

definitions.text: Casually unconcerned; breezily free of worry.
definitions.example: She strolled in insouciant, ordered for the whole table, and won the quiz without notes.

origin: From French insouciant, from in- (not) + souciant (worrying), from soucier (to worry), ultimately Latin sollicitare — the same restless root as solicit.

definitions.text: Causing gradual, subtle, and serious harm.
Wicked or destructive in a way that creeps rather than strikes.

origin: From Latin perniciosus, 'destructive,' from per- (thoroughly) + nex (death, slaughter). The damage arrives quietly, like a leak in the cellar.

definitions.text: Sparkling with wit, energy, or brilliance.
definitions.example: Scintillating conversation at table six tonight: someone is defending soup as a beverage.

origin: From Latin scintillare, 'to sparkle,' from scintilla (spark). Tinsel comes down from the same spark, via Old French estincele.

definitions.text: Slow, relaxed, and low on energy.
Faint or weak from heat or exhaustion.

origin: From Latin languidus, 'faint, weak,' from languere (to be weak) — the languish family. The word itself moves a little slowly.

definitions.text: Slow to understand; frustratingly dim.
Blunt or rounded; of an angle, greater than 90 degrees.

origin: From Latin obtusus, 'blunted,' from ob- (against) + tundere (to beat). A geometry term that wandered off and became an insult.

definitions.text: Untidy and rumpled, as if you just rolled out of bed.
In general disarray; mussed and unkempt.

origin: From Old French descheveler, 'to disarrange the hair,' from des- (apart) + chevel (hair). Bedhead is etymologically load-bearing.

definitions.text: Calm, even temper, especially under stress.
Mental composure; an untroubled, balanced mind.

origin: From Latin aequanimitas, from aequus (even, equal — as in equinox) + animus (mind, spirit). An even-keeled soul.

definitions.text: Reserved in speech; saying little by habit.
Habitually silent or uncommunicative.

origin: From Latin taciturnus, 'habitually silent,' from tacere (to be silent). Tacit agreement comes from the same root, minus the personality.

definitions.text: Dusk; the soft half-light after sunset.
definitions.example: We light the lamps at gloaming, and the arguments about darts begin.

origin: From Old English glomung, from glom (twilight, gloom). The day's last call for light.

definitions.text: Childishly sulky or bad-tempered over small slights.
Irritable and peevish; prone to petty moods.

origin: From Latin petulans, 'wanton, forward,' from petere (to attack, rush at). The tantrum is right there in the root.

definitions.text: Bubbly, enthusiastic, and full of life.
definitions.example: She is effervescent on quiz night — fizzes audibly at every right answer.

definitions.text: Giving off bubbles; fizzy.

origin: From Latin effervescere, 'to boil up,' from ex- (out) + fervescere (to begin to boil). The literal fizz came first; the personality followed.

definitions.text: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial things.
definitions.example: A garrulous stranger narrated his entire bus journey to me. I now know his sister's dog's birthday.

origin: From Latin garrulus, 'chattering,' from garrire (to chatter) — the same chattering, some say, as a goose.

definitions.text: Easily angered; hot-tempered by disposition.
Quick to flare, slow to cool.

origin: From Latin irascibilis, 'prone to anger,' from irasci (to grow angry), from ira (anger) — the same Ira that drives revenge tragedies.

definitions.text: So surprised or confused that you don't know how to react.
definitions.example: I was genuinely nonplussed when the Barkeep smiled. Did not know what to do with my hands.

origin: From Latin non plus, 'no more' — the state of having no further idea what to say. American usage increasingly flips it to mean 'unfazed,' which rather nonplusses everyone else.

definitions.text: Given to using very long words.
(Of a word) long and multisyllabic.

origin: From Latin sesquipedalis, 'a foot and a half long,' from sesqui- (one and a half) + pes (foot). Horace warned poets against such words; the word survived the warning.

definitions.text: A supposed cure for all problems.
A universal remedy; a fix for everything.

origin: From Greek panakeia, 'all-healing,' from pan- (all) + akos (cure). In Greek myth Panakeia was the goddess of universal remedy; in real life, the warranty expires.

definitions.text: Daily; ordinary, routine, everyday.
Happening every single day; commonplace.

origin: From Latin quotidianus, 'daily,' from quotidie (every day), from quot (how many) + dies (day). The everyday word wearing an elevated accent.

definitions.text: Offense or resentment, usually taken rather than given.
A shadow of displeasure; a sense of being slighted.

origin: From French umbrage, from Latin umbraticum (shade), from umbra (shadow). To take umbrage is to go sit in the shade and sulk.

definitions.text: Charming in an innocent, sweetly appealing way.
Attractive in a fresh, disarming fashion.

origin: From Old English wynsum, 'pleasant, joyful,' from wynn (joy, delight) + -sum (-some, as in awesome). Joy, distilled into an adjective.

definitions.text: The defining spirit or mood of a particular period of history.

origin: Borrowed from German Zeit (time) + Geist (spirit, ghost). The spirit of the age, briefly bottled.

definitions.text: Denoting a past period of idyllic calm and happiness.
definitions.example: Ah, the halcyon days of 2019, when standing shoulder-to-shoulder in a pub was considered boring.

origin: From Latin alcyon, from Greek alkyon (kingfisher). Myth held that the bird nested on a calm sea, and halcyon days were the windless weeks when its eggs hatched.

definitions.text: Using very few words; terse to the point of rudeness.
definitions.example: His review of the new bar across town? 'Wet.' Laconic, and somehow devastating.

definitions.text: Clipped, pithy, and brief.

origin: From Greek Lakonikos, 'of Laconia,' the Spartan homeland whose citizens were famously brief. Philip of Macedon allegedly warned Sparta that if he entered Laconia he would raze it. Their reply: 'If.'

definitions.text: Subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or mind.
definitions.example: The forecast was as mercurial as my landlord: sunshine at nine, hail by ten, an apology by noon.

definitions.text: Quick, lively, and hard to pin down.

origin: From Latin mercurialis, "of Mercury," the swift messenger god. Quicksilver never sits still, and neither does a mercurial person.

definitions.text: A devoted lover and collector of books.

origin: From Greek biblion (book) + philos (loving). The biblio- root also gives us Bible and bibliography.

definitions.text: A bad-tempered, surly person.
A cantankerous grump, often of the secretly affectionate variety.

origin: Of uncertain origin — possibly from French coeur méchant, 'evil heart,' though the evidence is thin. The word sounds exactly like what it describes, which is rarely an accident.

definitions.text: To move slowly and aimlessly; to waste time.
definitions.example: I dawdled on the walk over and lost the good fireside seats. Still worth it.

origin: Probably a variant of daddle (to waddle like a child); first recorded in the 1600s, wasting time ever since.

definitions.text: Intensely passionate; burning with zeal.
Heated in feeling or expression; glowing.

origin: From Latin fervidus, 'glowing, burning,' from fervere (to boil, glow). Fervent and fervor keep the same fire going.

definitions.text: Relating to the sense of taste.
Of or concerning the act of tasting.

origin: From Latin gustatorius, from gustare (to taste), from gustus (taste). Disgust is the same root, looking at the menu and walking away.

definitions.text: Too great, extreme, or sacred to be expressed in words.
Unutterable; beyond the reach of language.

origin: From Latin ineffabilis, 'unutterable,' from in- (not) + effari (to speak out), from ex- (out) + fari (to speak). Fable and fate are cousins on the same speaking root.

definitions.text: Rumor or gossip, especially of the informal clubhouse kind.
definitions.example: The scuttlebutt says the Barkeep entered a darts tournament under an assumed name. We shall see.

origin: Originally the cask (butt) with a hole (scuttle) for drinking water on a ship — where sailors naturally gathered to trade rumors. The gossip outlived the barrel.

definitions.text: Fiercely and bitterly critical; caustic.
definitions.example: The review was so vitriolic the chef framed it and hung it by the till.

origin: From Latin vitriolum (sulfuric acid), from vitrum (glass) — the glassy crystals the acid was first distilled from. Figurative acid tongue included.
